modalities.name: Look at Your Hand
modalities.tagline: Watch your own still hand until seeing and feeling come apart.
modalities.whatItIs: You rest one hand on a table, look at it and feel it at the same time, and notice how the 'hand' is made of separate, changing streams of sight and sensation. This proposed practice has no imagery, no story and no guide, just a real hand in front of you, and anyone can start it alone.
modalities.coreIdea: A familiar part of the body, looked at and felt closely, turns out to be a shifting mix of sights and sensations, and the practice is to watch that mix without adding anything.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit at a table in good light, rest one hand palm down and look at it for 15 minutes with soft, steady eyes. Every minute or so, switch between noticing only what you see (color, shadow, the faint movement of the pulse) and only what you feel (weight, warmth, tingling), and then notice both together. When thoughts or stories about your hand arise, let them go and come back to what is seen and felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation hard or drowsy, and anyone curious about how perception is put together.
modalities.cautions: Long, close looking can sometimes make a familiar body part seem strange or unreal, so look away, move the hand and stop if that feels unsettling. People with a history of dissociation or psychosis should check with a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Can't meditate with eyes closed? Look at Your Hand was invented for that: rest it on a table, then for 15 minutes notice only what you see, then only what you feel, then both. A real hand, watched closely, may turn out to be busy.

modalities.name: The Small Sway
modalities.tagline: Sit upright and feel the body's tiny, constant balancing.
modalities.whatItIs: In The Small Sway you sit upright on a stool without a backrest and feel the tiny, constant movements the body makes to keep its balance: a lean, a catch, a settle, many times a minute. There are no inner voices to meet and no parts to talk to, only one body quietly balancing itself, watched as plain sensation. It is a proposed, calm practice that can be learned from a short guide and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Even sitting still, the body is never quite still, and noticing its endless small corrections is meant to show balance as something that keeps happening rather than a fixed state.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit on a firm stool or the front edge of a chair for 15 to 20 minutes, feet flat, back upright but not stiff, eyes half open. Notice the slight sways forward, back and to the sides, the small tightenings in the belly and back that catch them, and the moments of settling, without trying to stop or steady them. If the sway grows or you feel dizzy, lean back against something or stop.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find breath or emotions too subtle or too loaded as a focus, and meditators curious about the movement hidden in stillness.
modalities.cautions: Use a stable seat and stop if you feel dizzy, faint or unsteady, especially if you have balance problems or low blood pressure. Even short sits can now and then stir up unsettling feelings; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Sitting still? Your body is still swaying, catching and settling many times a minute. Feel it in The Small Sway: sit upright on a stool for 15 minutes and notice that tiny balancing without trying to stop it. Untested; stop if you feel dizzy.

modalities.name: Tension, Untouched
modalities.tagline: Watch tense spots change without relaxing them on purpose.
modalities.whatItIs: This practice watches the body's tense spots, such as a tight jaw, raised shoulders or a clenched hand, under one firm rule: you do not relax them on purpose. Relaxation methods and cognitive behavioral therapy both set out to change something; this proposed practice changes nothing and simply sees what tension does by itself. It is self-led and loosely structured.
modalities.coreIdea: Tension shifts, spreads and eases on its own more often than we notice, and leaving it entirely alone is meant to let that be seen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie for 20 minutes and find the most noticeable tension in the body, such as the jaw, shoulders, hands or belly. Stay with it and watch what it does over the minutes, and whenever you catch yourself starting to relax it deliberately, let that intention go too. When it changes or fades on its own, find the next tense spot.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always trying to relax and find the trying itself tiring, and meditators curious about how tension behaves when it is left alone.
modalities.cautions: Do not use this with pain from an injury, new or worsening pain or a medical condition, and move or stretch whenever you need to. It is an untested idea; if tension or anxiety feels constant, talk to a doctor.
modalities.tweet: Tight jaw, raised shoulders? Don't relax them. Watch each tense spot for 20 minutes and see what it does when nobody tries to make it let go. That speculative practice is called Tension, Untouched. Skip it for pain from an injury.

modalities.name: Body Rhythms Watch
modalities.tagline: Watch the body's own rhythms start and end by themselves.
modalities.whatItIs: One after another, in a set order, you watch the body's natural rhythms (breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking) as cycles that start and end on their own. Body Rhythms Watch is wordless and still, with no metaphors, no values to clarify and nothing to decide or do, and this proposed practice can be learned from a teacher or a book.
modalities.coreIdea: The body is full of rhythms that rise and fall without your help, and watching them closely is meant to show change happening by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still for 25 minutes and spend about five minutes on each rhythm in a set order: the rise and fall of the breath, the pulse felt in the chest or fingertips, the urge and act of swallowing, the blink of the eyes, and finally all of them together. For each one you watch where a cycle begins and where it ends, without speeding it up or slowing it down. If a rhythm is hard to find, you simply rest with the previous one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer quiet bodily practice to talking, and meditators who want a calm, structured way to watch change in the body.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to heartbeat or breathing can make some people anxious, especially with panic attacks or heart worries, so skip those rhythms or switch to sounds if that happens. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for medical advice about heart or breathing symptoms.
modalities.tweet: Your body keeps time all day without you. In Body Rhythms Watch you sit still and spend five minutes each on breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking, watching each cycle start and end by itself. New and untested; if the pulse makes you uneasy, skip it.

modalities.name: Whenever It Rains
modalities.tagline: When rain comes, sit by a window and watch the drops.
modalities.whatItIs: On rainy days you sit by a window and watch single drops land, run and disappear. No meaning is sought, no feelings are dug into and no past is involved; Whenever It Rains is a proposed, calm, self-led practice that needs nothing but a window.
modalities.coreIdea: Rain is a ready-made, meaningless display of things arising and passing, and watching it with plain attention is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: When it rains, sit by a window for 15 to 20 minutes, choose one patch of glass and follow single drops: where each lands, how it runs, joins others and vanishes. When the mind drifts into stories or plans, notice that and pick a new drop. For the last few minutes add the sound of the rain, listening to each patter begin and end.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find formal meditation dry and would like a practice tied to everyday life, and anyone who already loves watching the rain.
modalities.cautions: Gray, rainy days can lower some people's mood, so stop if it starts to feel gloomy rather than calm, and talk to a doctor if low mood lasts. It is an untested idea, and even calm meditation can occasionally stir up difficult feelings.
modalities.tweet: Rainy day? Whenever It Rains is a hypothetical practice: sit by a window, pick one patch of glass and follow single drops as they land, run and vanish. No meaning to find, no story to tell. Just rain, coming and going.

modalities.name: Edges of Thought
modalities.tagline: Catch the exact moment each thought begins and ends.
modalities.whatItIs: Edges of Thought is a proposed insight meditation that takes thinking itself as its object, watching for the moment each thought begins and the moment it dissolves. The body stays still while attention turns to the mind, the reverse of practices where the body leads and shakes. It is calm and structured, and it is usually learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Thoughts are events with edges, and noticing where they start and stop, rather than what they say, is meant to show how quickly they come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and wait, alert but relaxed, for the next thought to appear, the way a cat waits by a mouse hole. When one appears, note 'start' without following its content, and then note 'gone' when it fades or turns into another thought. Between thoughts, rest in whatever quiet or sensation is there until the next one arrives.
modalities.whoItsFor: People caught up in busy thinking who are curious about how thoughts actually behave, and meditators who want to add the mind to body-based insight practice.
modalities.cautions: Watching thoughts closely can at first make them seem louder or faster, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it feels agitating. If intrusive or distressing thoughts dominate, talk with a professional, and people with a history of psychosis should check with a clinician first; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Can you catch a thought starting? In the untested Edges of Thought, you sit still and wait for the next thought like a cat at a mouse hole, note 'start' when it appears and 'gone' when it fades, and never follow what it says.

modalities.name: The Body Surveyor
modalities.tagline: Measure each sensation's size and place, as a surveyor would.
modalities.whatItIs: Each sensation is measured the way a surveyor measures land: its exact size, position and edges, then measured again a minute later. The Body Surveyor never asks what a sensation means or what it is trying to say, only where it is and how big; it is a proposed practice, learned from a teacher and then done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Measuring a sensation precisely tends to show that its size and edges keep changing, which may turn a vague bodily sense into a clearer view of change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and pick the most noticeable sensation, such as pressure in the seat or warmth in the palms. Estimate it like a surveyor (its size in centimeters, its exact location, its sharpest and fuzziest edges), then wait a minute and measure again, noting any change in a word. Move to the next sensation after three or four measurements.
modalities.whoItsFor: Precise, practical people who find open-ended body awareness too vague, and meditators curious about how fixed sensations really are.
modalities.cautions: Close, repeated attention to an uncomfortable spot can make it feel stronger at first, so move on if it does, and never use it on new, sharp or worsening pain. It is an untested idea, and people with a history of trauma or dissociation should start with short sessions.
modalities.tweet: Pick one sensation, like pressure in the seat, and estimate its size and edges the way a surveyor would. Measure again a minute later. It rarely stays the same size. The Body Surveyor turns that into an experimental sit, with short rounds to start.

modalities.name: A Week Around the Body
modalities.tagline: Seven body regions, one for each day's whole sit.
modalities.whatItIs: A printed seven-day chart gives each day one body region, the hands on Monday, the feet on Tuesday, the face on Wednesday and so on, and that region is the only object of the whole day's sit. You run it yourself, week after week, with no coach and no variation; A Week Around the Body is an untested, rigidly structured practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Spending a whole sit on one region, and returning to it a week later, is meant to show how much one small part of the body holds and how differently it shows up each time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each day, sit for 20 minutes and rest attention only on the day's region (hands, feet, face, belly, back, shoulders, then the whole body on the seventh day), noticing whatever sensations are there without moving on. After the sit, write one line on the chart. After four weeks, read across each row to compare the same region week by week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like a fixed, simple schedule they can keep alone, and meditators who find moving through the whole body in one sit too hurried.
modalities.cautions: Staying a whole sit with one region can bring numbness or strong sensations, especially where there was past injury or trauma, so swap the region or open your eyes if needed. The practice works only with present sensation and never looks for forgotten events, any memory that surfaces is not evidence of what happened, and even a short daily sit can sometimes stir difficult feelings; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Monday the hands, Tuesday the feet, Wednesday the face. In A Week Around the Body, each day's 20-minute sit stays with one body region, one line goes on a chart, and the same region comes back next week. Untested so far; swap regions if one feels too much.

modalities.name: Three Grades of Effort
modalities.tagline: Sit with light, then moderate, then strong effort, and compare.
modalities.whatItIs: In Three Grades of Effort a teacher leads three back-to-back sits on the same object, each with a deliberately different amount of effort: light, moderate and strong. Instead of dropping all control, as Do Nothing meditation does, you vary it on purpose and study what each grade does to what you notice. It is a proposed, structured practice in a small silent group.
modalities.coreIdea: Effort shapes what meditation shows you, and comparing grades of effort side by side is meant to turn effort itself into something you can observe and adjust.
modalities.whatYouDo: The teacher sets one object, such as sensations in the hands, and three 15-minute sits: the first with the lightest possible attention, the second with steady, moderate attention and the third with strong, close, effortful attention. After each sit you write a few words on what you noticed, how clear it was and how tiring it felt. The session ends with a short talk with the teacher comparing the three.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who are unsure whether they try too hard or not hard enough, and people who like structured, experiment-like practice.
modalities.cautions: Strong effort in meditation can bring headaches, tension or unsettling experiences, so keep the strong grade short and ease off if it becomes uncomfortable. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Untested: Three Grades of Effort. Light, moderate, strong: three back-to-back sits on the same object, each with a different amount of effort, then a talk with the teacher about what each one showed you. Keep the strong grade short.

modalities.name: Low Battery Sitting
modalities.tagline: When you are already tired, sit and watch the tiredness itself.
modalities.whatItIs: Low Battery Sitting is for the times you are already worn out, such as the afternoon slump or the end of a long day: instead of pushing through or perking yourself up, you sit and watch what the tiredness is made of. Interval training spends energy on purpose and asks you to push; this proposed practice asks for no effort at all and simply studies a low-energy state as it comes and goes. It is learned from a meditation teacher and then done alone, with only a few loose guidelines.
modalities.coreIdea: Tiredness feels like one solid weight, but looked at closely it may turn out to be a changing mix of heavy limbs, blurred thoughts, yawns and small waves of alertness, and seeing that without fighting it or feeding it is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: When you notice you are tired, sit or recline somewhere safe for 15 to 20 minutes with eyes half closed, and let attention go to whatever is most obvious about the tiredness: heavy eyelids or limbs, foggy or drifting thoughts, a yawn building, the pull toward coffee or your phone. Do not try to wake yourself up or to relax more deeply; just notice each part as it rises and fades, including the moments when the fog thins on its own. If you doze off, that is fine: when you come back, notice the moment of waking and end the sit there.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always fight tiredness with caffeine, screens or willpower, and meditators who treat sleepiness as an obstacle and are curious to make it the object instead.
modalities.cautions: Never practice while driving, cooking or in charge of anything that needs you alert, and get up slowly afterward. Tiredness that lasts for weeks, comes with low mood or follows poor sleep night after night is worth raising with a doctor, since this untested idea is not a treatment for fatigue, insomnia or depression.
modalities.tweet: Tired? Don't push through or perk up. Sit for 15 minutes and watch what the tiredness is made of: heavy eyelids, foggy thoughts, a yawn building, the fog thinning on its own. Untested so far, Low Battery Sitting should never be tried while driving.

modalities.name: Crowded Empty Room
modalities.tagline: Alone in a room, notice how often the mind brings people in.
modalities.whatItIs: Alone in a quiet room, how often does the mind bring other people in? Crowded Empty Room watches exactly that: imagined conversations, replayed chats, planned replies, with no teammates, no game and no one to react to. This proposed practice is learned from a teacher who checks in now and then.
modalities.coreIdea: Even alone, the mind stays busy with other people, and seeing that clearly, without joining the conversations, is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 25 minutes and rest attention on the sensations of sitting. Each time the mind brings someone in (a conversation, a face, a reply you are drafting), you silently note 'people', notice how it feels in the body and return to sitting. Every couple of weeks you tell your teacher what you noticed, such as which people visit most often.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay conversations or rehearse what they will say, and meditators curious about the social side of the mind.
modalities.cautions: Replayed conversations can stir loneliness, resentment or rumination, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it gets heavy. Solitary practice is not a replacement for real contact if you are isolated or lonely; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Alone in a room, your head can still be crowded. Crowded Empty Room is a new idea: 25 minutes of solitude, and each time an imagined conversation or replayed chat shows up, note 'people' and come back to sitting. Shorten it if it gets heavy.

modalities.name: Many Short Beginnings
modalities.tagline: A sit broken into short rounds, each one started fresh.
modalities.whatItIs: A teacher-led sit is broken into 90-second rounds, each ended by a bell after which you stand, sit down again and begin completely afresh. Nothing in Many Short Beginnings is sustained or built up over time; the practice is beginning, again and again, and this proposed format is run by a teacher in person or by recording.
modalities.coreIdea: The first moments of a sit are often the most alert and curious, and restarting many times is meant to keep attention in that fresh state instead of settling into a long, dulling effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the bell, sit and notice whatever is most obvious (sounds, sensations or thoughts) as if for the first time. At the next bell, 90 seconds later, stand up, take a breath, sit down and start again with nothing carried over from the last round. Twelve rounds make a session of about 25 minutes, followed by a short check-in with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get dull or sleepy in long sits, and meditators who want to study the freshness of beginning.
modalities.cautions: Standing up and sitting down again and again can make some people dizzy, so rise slowly, or stay seated and simply open your eyes at each bell. Meditation can sometimes bring up difficult experiences, so people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: When a sit turns dull or sleepy, try an untested format, Many Short Beginnings: twelve fresh starts in 25 minutes. At each bell you stand, sit down again and begin completely afresh, with nothing carried over. Rise slowly, or just open your eyes.

modalities.name: Ownerless Moments
modalities.tagline: Notice how much happens on its own, without a doer.
modalities.whatItIs: This teacher-guided practice notices how much of experience simply happens: sounds arrive, thoughts appear and the breath goes on, with no one making them happen. Ownerless Moments is calm and effortless, exploring experience without a doer rather than building a sense of 'I can', and this proposed practice needs an experienced teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Much of experience seems to arrive by itself, and this practice explores that directly, without effort or control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and let attention rest on whatever is most obvious. Instead of thinking 'I hear' or 'I am breathing', you silently note 'hearing happens', 'breathing happens' or 'thinking happens', and notice whether any controller can actually be found. The teacher meets you weekly to talk through what you noticed and to adjust or pause the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced meditators curious about the Buddhist idea of not-self, and people who feel worn out by always having to be in control.
modalities.cautions: This can feel unsettling, as if things are unreal or you are detached from yourself, so stop, open your eyes, move and talk to someone if that happens. People with a history of dissociation, depersonalization or psychosis should avoid it unless a clinician agrees; it is an untested concept and needs an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: Who is doing the hearing? Ownerless Moments is a teacher-guided concept: note 'hearing happens' and 'thinking happens', and check whether any controller can be found. Calm and effortless, but not for everyone, so do it with a teacher.

modalities.name: Left Side, Right Side
modalities.tagline: Left hand, right hand: compare matched body parts on a fixed beat.
modalities.whatItIs: A short printed list of matched body parts and an interval timer are all you need: every 30 seconds attention switches from the left side to the right and back, so each part of the body is compared with its twin. Where animal-assisted work depends on a companion and a trained handler, Left Side, Right Side needs nobody at all, and its fixed list and timing can be learned from one page; it is a proposed, solitary practice.
modalities.coreIdea: The two sides of the body are rarely felt exactly the same, and switching between matched parts on a fixed beat is meant to make the small, shifting differences between them easy to notice, with nothing outside you to compare against.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still for 20 minutes with eyes closed and an interval timer set to chime every 30 seconds. Work down the list in its fixed order, giving each pair two minutes (left hand, right hand, left hand, right hand, then the feet, knees, hips, shoulders, ears, the sides of the face and the eyes), and at the end of each pair silently note which side felt more vivid, or 'even'. In the last four minutes, feel both sides at once and notice where the body feels lopsided and where it feels balanced.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a clear, timed routine they can run alone with nothing but a list and a timer, and meditators curious about how unevenly the body is actually felt.
modalities.cautions: Small differences between the sides are common and usually mean nothing, but sudden numbness, weakness or tingling on one side, or a drooping face, is an emergency, so stop and get urgent medical help. Meditation can sometimes stir up difficult experiences, so keep the first sessions short and stop if it becomes unsettling; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Is your left hand as vivid as your right? A timer chimes every 30 seconds while attention switches sides, pair by pair, from the hands to the feet to the face. All Left Side, Right Side needs is a list and a timer, and it's still untested.

modalities.name: When a Song Gets Stuck
modalities.tagline: Watch a stuck song loop and fade, without trying to stop it.
modalities.whatItIs: When a tune loops in your head on its own, you neither hum it away nor drown it out: you sit and watch it repeat, change and eventually fade. When a Song Gets Stuck regulates nothing, not the breath, not the body and not the song, the far side from practices that coordinate all three; this proposed practice is learned from a book or a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: A stuck song is a vivid, everyday example of the mind producing something by itself, and watching it without resistance is meant to show how such loops come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: When a tune is stuck, sit or stand still for 10 minutes and listen to it inwardly as if it were playing in the room. Notice which fragment repeats, whether it speeds up, slows or changes, the moments it drops out and comes back, and any irritation along the way, all without singing along or trying to push it out. End when it fades or the time is up, whichever comes first.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are often bothered by tunes stuck in their heads, and meditators curious about how the mind runs on its own.
modalities.cautions: This is for ordinary stuck songs; if intrusive sounds, voices or repetitive thoughts are distressing or feel out of your control, talk to a doctor or mental health professional rather than practicing with them. People with a history of psychosis should check with a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Got a song stuck in your head? Don't hum it away. Sit for 10 minutes and watch it loop, change and fade on its own. When a Song Gets Stuck: a novel, simple look at how the mind runs by itself.

modalities.name: Keep It to Yourself
modalities.tagline: Thirty days of sitting you never describe to anyone.
modalities.whatItIs: For a month of daily insight sits you follow one unusual rule: you never describe what you experience to anyone, not friends, not social media and not a journal. Socializing turns experience into shared stories; Keep It to Yourself keeps it private and unnarrated inside a strict, teacher-set structure, with a weekly safety check as the only exception.
modalities.coreIdea: Telling others about an experience starts to shape it into a story, and leaving it untold is meant to keep attention on the experience itself rather than on how it will sound.
modalities.whatYouDo: For 30 days, sit for 30 minutes at a fixed time, slowly sweeping attention through the body as the teacher has set out. Afterwards you say nothing, write nothing and post nothing about it. Each week the teacher asks you one question, 'is anything difficult coming up?', and you answer honestly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice they experience things partly in order to tell others about them, and meditators who share every insight and want to try the opposite.
modalities.cautions: The rule never covers distress: if anything frightening, painful or overwhelming comes up, tell the teacher, a friend or a professional at once. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What happens to an experience you never describe? Keep It to Yourself is a thought experiment: a 30-day sitting practice where you tell no one, post nothing and write nothing. One exception: anything difficult always gets shared.

modalities.name: One Clock, Sixty Ticks
modalities.tagline: Sixty ticks of an ordinary clock, each heard as new.
modalities.whatItIs: The most regular sound in a house, the tick of an analog clock, followed for exactly sixty ticks at a time: that is the object of One Clock, Sixty Ticks. The setting is fixed, man-made and perfectly regular, and the point of this proposed, teacher-set practice is to notice that even identical ticks are never heard quite the same way twice.
modalities.coreIdea: A sound that never varies makes the variation in your own hearing and attention easy to notice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit near a ticking analog clock with eyes closed and follow sixty ticks, counting them and noticing how each one starts, sounds and fades. Rest for a minute, then repeat for five rounds, each time noticing what differs: loudness, sharpness, the pauses, your own wandering. Once a month you review your observations with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like simple, exact instructions, and meditators curious about how much changes inside even when nothing outside changes.
modalities.cautions: Focusing on a repetitive sound can feel irritating or, for some people, anxious, so stop if it does. People with tinnitus or sound sensitivity may prefer another object, and as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Sixty ticks of an ordinary clock, five rounds, eyes closed. The clock never changes, so you get to notice how your hearing does. One Clock, Sixty Ticks: an untested indoor practice in plain listening.

modalities.name: Three-Line Insight Journal
modalities.tagline: Three short written lines after each sit, reviewed with a teacher.
modalities.whatItIs: After each structured sit you write three short lines on classic themes of insight meditation, in plain words: change, dissatisfaction and the absence of a fixed self. The Three-Line Insight Journal adds reflection, words and a teacher's guidance to plain sensing, and this proposed practice suits people who make sense of experience by writing.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing a few plain lines after each sit can turn fleeting observations into a clearer understanding over the weeks.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 20-minute sit, write three lines: one thing you saw change, one moment when something did not satisfy or you wanted more, and one thing that happened by itself without you doing it. Keep the lines short and descriptive rather than analytical. Every two weeks, read the journal through with a teacher, who helps you notice patterns.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think best on paper, and meditators who want guidance in making sense of what they notice.
modalities.cautions: Reflection can slide into rumination or harsh self-judgment, so keep each line short and factual and skip the writing on days it feels heavy. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for therapy if hard material keeps coming up.
modalities.tweet: Meditators who think on paper might like this proposed habit: after each sit, write one thing that changed, one moment of wanting more, and one thing that happened by itself. The Three-Line Insight Journal gets a teacher review every two weeks.

modalities.name: Listening for Silence
modalities.tagline: Listen to the silence itself, and let sounds come and go.
modalities.whatItIs: The quiet itself is the object here, with sounds appearing and vanishing against it like visitors. Listening for Silence has no melody, rhythm or company, only everyday sounds and the silence around them; this proposed practice is calm, structured and stays in the present.
modalities.coreIdea: Silence is always there between and beneath sounds, and resting in it is meant to show every sound as something that begins, lasts a moment and ends.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 20 minutes with eyes closed, and for the first few minutes simply listen to whatever sounds are there, such as a distant car, a fridge hum or your own breath. Then shift attention to the silence around and between them, noting 'sound' when one arrives and 'silence' when it has gone. In the last five minutes, rest in the quiet itself and let any sound pass through without following it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love listening or feel crowded by constant noise, and anyone who wants a quiet, simple insight practice without music or spoken guidance.
modalities.cautions: In very quiet rooms, ringing in the ears (tinnitus) or sound sensitivity can become more noticeable or distressing, so stop or add gentle background sound if that happens. Meditation can occasionally bring up difficult experiences, and people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new idea, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: No music, no voice, just the quiet underneath. Spend 20 minutes alone letting each sound arrive and fade while attention rests on the silence it came from. Listening for Silence: an untested practice for noise-weary ears.

modalities.name: Solid Finish Sprints
modalities.tagline: Every hard burst ends with both palms on something solid.
modalities.whatItIs: Solid Finish Sprints is a proposed solo interval session in which every hard burst runs to a sturdy, real object, such as a broad tree trunk or a sturdy fence post, and ends with both palms resting flat against it. It takes HIIT further from the Ideal Parent Figure Protocol, which meets distress with imagined, comforting figures: here the peak of each effort lands only on something physical that is actually there, felt through the hands and seen up close, with no imagery, no guide and no comfort added.
modalities.coreIdea: Ending each burst in plain contact with a solid object is meant to give the hardest moment a concrete, outward landing point, so attention may stay with the real world at the very moment the body is working hardest.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up of easy jogging and leg swings, you pick five or six sturdy objects spread around a flat, open park, each 40 to 80 meters from the next, and run hard from one to the next for about 10 to 15 seconds, easing off over the last few strides so that you arrive at a walk. At each one you rest both palms on it for twenty breaths, noticing its texture, temperature and grain, then run on to the next, going round the circuit twice before five minutes of easy walking to cool down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already exercise hard and find their minds drifting into self-talk or replayed worries during intervals, and anyone who wants a plain, device-free session to run alone in a park.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting, high blood pressure or joint problems, build a base of easier exercise before going near your hardest, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Never run at walls, glass or thorny, sharp or slippery objects, always slow to a walk before you touch, keep to dry, even ground away from traffic and other people, and remember that this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Sprint to a tree, slow to a walk over the last strides, rest both palms on the bark for twenty breaths, then sprint on to the next tree or post. Solid Finish Sprints is an untested idea: hard effort always lands on something real. Doctor check first.

modalities.name: The Signed Card
modalities.tagline: Decide the whole session in advance, then simply follow it.
modalities.whatItIs: The night before, you write the exact session on a card, including firm safety stop rules, sign it and then follow it to the letter. With one decision made in advance, The Signed Card leaves no room for bargaining between competing inner voices during the effort; it is a proposed, fully structured routine done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Deciding once, calmly and in advance, is meant to take the bargaining out of the hard moments, while pre-written safety rules keep your body's real warning signs in charge.
modalities.whatYouDo: The evening before, write the session on a card, for example a 10-minute warm-up, six 1-minute hard bouts on a bike with 2 minutes easy between, and a cool-down, plus stop rules such as chest pain, dizziness or sharp joint pain. Sign it and leave it where you will see it. During the session, thoughts like 'skip the last one' are noticed and let go, and only the stop rules can change the plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often talk themselves out of workouts halfway through, and anyone who likes the clarity of a commitment made in advance.
modalities.cautions: The stop rules always beat the card: halt at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain, and get medical advice before hard exercise if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or another serious condition. Build up gradually with easy days between sessions; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Write tomorrow's interval session on a card tonight, with firm stop rules for pain or dizziness, sign it, then follow it exactly, with no bargaining mid-workout. The Signed Card is a new idea: decide once, not every minute, and the stop rules always win.

modalities.name: Too Hard to Think
modalities.tagline: Let hard effort crowd out thinking, then notice the quiet.
modalities.whatItIs: This interval practice uses hard bouts as a deliberate break from thinking: attention goes entirely to the raw sensations of effort, and each recovery is spent noticing how quiet the mind may have become. In Too Hard to Think, thoughts are not examined or questioned at all, only crowded out for a while, with no self-talk, no analysis and no scorekeeping.
modalities.coreIdea: During very hard effort many people find little room left for thinking, and the session uses that on purpose as a short, physical holiday from the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, a rower or a track, do six to eight hard bouts of 30 to 60 seconds, and during each one put all your attention on the burning legs, the heavy breathing and the pounding heart. During each two-minute easy recovery, notice how quiet or busy the mind is, without judging it. Cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overthink and want a physical break from their own thoughts, and anyone who finds sitting meditation too hard to settle into.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, build a base before hard bouts and stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. It is an untested idea that does not replace care for anxiety or persistent worry, so seek help if worry or low mood lasts.
modalities.tweet: Hard effort can leave little room for thinking. Too Hard to Think is a speculative practice that uses this on purpose: put all attention on burning legs and heavy breath during each bout, then notice how quiet your mind is while you recover.

modalities.name: Meter by Meter
modalities.tagline: One number per session, nudged up in tiny steps.
modalities.whatItIs: Meter by Meter is a self-run interval program built around one measured score per session, such as meters rowed in each 30-second bout, which you aim to nudge up by tiny amounts over weeks. It steers entirely by that number and aims straight at changing the body, with no values talk or feelings work involved. It is an untested concept, fully structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: A visible score that creeps upward makes progress concrete, as long as the steps stay tiny and a bad day counts as data rather than failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Warm up for 10 minutes on a rowing machine, then row eight 30-second hard bouts with 90 seconds easy between, noting the meters for each bout. Write the average on a scoreboard on your wall, and next session aim to beat it by one or two meters at most, or simply match it. Every fourth week is an easier week with no target.
modalities.whoItsFor: People motivated by numbers and visible progress, and anyone who wants proof on paper that their training is going somewhere.
modalities.cautions: Chasing a number can push you into overreaching, injury or poor form, so keep the steps tiny, take the easy weeks and stop a bout if your technique breaks down. Get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or back problems, and stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Eight hard 30-second rows, your average meters on a scoreboard, and next time you try to beat it by a meter or two. Meter by Meter builds a new concept on tiny steps, an easy week every fourth week and progress you can see. Stop a bout if form breaks.

modalities.name: Let the Pulse Decide
modalities.tagline: Your pulse, not the clock, decides when the next bout starts.
modalities.whatItIs: In Let the Pulse Decide, each rest lasts exactly as long as your heart needs: the next hard bout starts only when your pulse falls back to a set number. There is no meaning to find and no story to tell, just a present-moment signal from the body deciding what happens next. It is a proposed, self-led session that needs only a watch or a heart rate monitor.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting recovery, not a fixed timer, set the rest keeps each session matched to how your body is doing that day.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before starting, pick a recovery pulse, such as the heart rate you have during brisk walking. After a 10-minute warm-up, do a 1-minute hard bout on a bike or on foot, then move easily until your pulse, counted at the wrist for 10 seconds or read from a monitor, falls to that number, and only then start the next bout. Stop after six to eight bouts, or sooner if recovery starts taking twice as long as it did at the beginning.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like listening to their bodies, and anyone whose energy varies a lot from day to day and who wants sessions that adjust by themselves.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, chest pain or fainting, or take medicines that affect heart rate, since these can make pulse targets misleading. Wrist monitors can be inaccurate during hard effort, so also go by how you feel, stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Experimental twist on intervals: Let the Pulse Decide. After each hard minute, recover until your pulse drops back to a set number, and only then go again. Your heart sets the rest, not the clock, so each session fits the day you're having.

modalities.name: Split to the Second
modalities.tagline: Hit a target time to the second, again and again.
modalities.whatItIs: You run or row a fixed distance again and again, aiming to hit a target time within one second while a partner calls out your times: the goal is accuracy, not top speed. Split to the Second turns every repeat into a test of how well you can judge your own effort against the clock, far from a body left to shake on its own, and in this proposed session the effort stays hard but measured.
modalities.coreIdea: Landing the same time again and again while working hard asks you to judge effort accurately against the clock, so the body does exactly what you choose rather than whatever it would do on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, run 200 meters on a track or row 250 meters, aiming for a target time that feels hard but repeatable, such as 50 seconds, with 90 seconds of walking or easy rowing between. A partner calls each time, and you adjust your pace to land within one second of the target. Do six to ten repeats and finish with an easy cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and skill, and those who tend to start too fast and fade, who want to judge their pace accurately under effort.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and build up slowly to avoid strains, especially in the calves and hamstrings. Keep targets hard but not all-out, stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain, and rest between hard days; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Not faster, more exact. Run 200 m (or row 250 m) again and again, trying to land the same target time within one second while a partner calls it out. Split to the Second: an untested session in hard effort and exact pacing.

modalities.name: Call Your Effort
modalities.tagline: Name your effort as a number, then check how close you were.
modalities.whatItIs: Call Your Effort is a proposed interval session in which you state an exact effort level out loud before every bout, such as 'eight out of ten', and afterward check it against your heart rate or distance and your honest sense of how it went. Vague bodily impressions become crisp, stated numbers, the reverse of waiting patiently for a felt sense to clarify. Over weeks, the aim is to call your effort accurately.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people misjudge how hard they are working, and practicing precise calls, checked against measurements, is meant to sharpen that judgment.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or rower, call a target before each of eight 1-minute bouts, mixing levels such as six, eight and nine out of ten, with 2 minutes easy between. After each bout, note your heart rate or distance and your honest rating of how it felt, and compare the call with the result. Over weeks, track how often your call and your result match.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always go too hard or never hard enough, and anyone who wants to learn to read their own effort without relying on a gadget.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and keep nines and tens to a few short bouts once you have built a base. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and keep easy days between sessions; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Eight out of ten, or really six? Say your target effort before each bout, then check it against your heart rate and how it really felt. The proposal in Call Your Effort is to learn to judge hard work accurately. Medical advice first.

modalities.name: The Last Bout Counts
modalities.tagline: Every session is built around how well you finish.
modalities.whatItIs: In The Last Bout Counts, only the final hard bout of each session is measured and rated, and everything before it is designed as preparation for finishing well. It is a closed, self-run plan aimed squarely at one change, holding quality to the very end, rather than an open process that unfolds with a coach. It is a proposed program done alone, two or three times a week.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people fade badly by the end of hard efforts, and making the finish the one thing that counts is meant to train pacing, patience and composure under fatigue.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or rower, do five 1-minute bouts with 2 minutes easy between, holding the first four slightly below your best on purpose. Give the fifth your best controlled effort, then record its distance or power and a 1 to 10 rating of how composed you felt. Adjust the first four next time so the last one comes out strongest, and cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who start too hard and fall apart, and anyone who wants to practice finishing well rather than starting fast.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build a base of easier exercise before hard bouts. A best final effort should still be controlled, never to the point of collapse, so stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Do you fade by the end? The Last Bout Counts flips the usual plan: five hard minutes where only the last one is measured, and the first four are paced to set it up. An untested way to practice finishing well.

modalities.name: Count Back by Threes
modalities.tagline: Hard effort for the body, a small puzzle for the mind.
modalities.whatItIs: This partner session keeps body and mind busy at once: during every hard bout, a partner who is not exercising gives you a simple mental task, such as counting back from 100 in threes, which you answer aloud between breaths. Count Back by Threes is the opposite of letting everything be, a proposed session in which nothing in you is left idle. It is fully structured and learned from a coach first.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing a simple mental task while working hard asks for full engagement of body and attention together, and the idea is that practicing both at once trains composure when things are demanding.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, do six 30-second hard bouts on a bike or rower with 90 seconds easy between, while your partner stands beside you. During each bout the partner gives one task (count back in threes from a random number, name animals from A to Z, spell a word backwards) and you answer aloud, slowly if needed. Cool down for 10 minutes, then swap roles and run your partner's session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find hard intervals mindless or boring, and anyone curious to see how their thinking holds up under effort.
modalities.cautions: Keep the tasks simple, and because your attention is split, the partner also watches your form and any warning signs and calls a stop if you look dizzy, confused or more breathless than normal hard effort. Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Count back from 100 in threes. Now do it in the middle of a hard 30-second bout. That is the untested partner session called Count Back by Threes: your body works flat out while a partner hands your mind a small puzzle and watches for warning signs.

modalities.name: Shift on Command
modalities.tagline: Practice shifting your state on command: easy, hard, flat-out.
modalities.whatItIs: Three gears (easy, hard and flat-out) are switched on a fixed schedule through one continuous session. Instead of watching your state change by itself, in Shift on Command you change it yourself, again and again, on cue; this proposed session works alone with a timer or with a partner calling the gears.
modalities.coreIdea: Shifting up and down on command, many times in one session, practices a deliberate kind of control over how activated you are.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or a rower, work through a 3-minute block of 90 seconds easy, 60 seconds hard and 30 seconds flat-out, then repeat the block five or six times without stopping. The skill is in the transitions: hitting each new gear quickly and cleanly, and especially dropping back to easy right away. Finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to switch on or to switch off, and anyone who wants a workout that trains control rather than just endurance.
modalities.cautions: Flat-out efforts strain the heart and muscles, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up with the easy and hard gears before adding flat-out. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and keep easy days between sessions; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Easy, hard, flat-out, repeat: 90 seconds, 60, 30, five or six times without stopping. In this untested session the skill is the shifting itself, especially dropping back to easy fast. Shift on Command adds the flat-out gear last. #HIIT

modalities.name: The Preflight Check
modalities.tagline: A fixed solo checklist before every hard session, like a pilot's.
modalities.whatItIs: Every hard session begins with a fixed, written readiness checklist, the way a pilot checks a plane before take-off. On a team, coaches and teammates often notice when you are tired, ill or hurting; training alone, The Preflight Check does that job, and only when every item passes does this proposed routine go on to the hard bouts.
modalities.coreIdea: A short, honest checklist done every time is meant to catch the days when hard effort is a bad idea, which matters most when no one else is watching.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each session, answer six questions on a card: slept reasonably, eaten and drunk, no illness or fever, no new or sharp pain, no recent chest discomfort or dizziness, and calm enough to stop if needed. If any answer is no, you swap the session for an easy walk. If all pass, warm up for 10 minutes and do six to eight 30-second hard bouts on a bike or rower with 90 seconds easy between, then cool down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who train alone and tend to push through warning signs, and anyone who wants a simple safety habit around hard exercise.
modalities.cautions: A checklist does not replace medical advice, so get that first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up gradually from easier exercise. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness even if the checklist passed, and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Pilots check the plane before every flight. Before each solo hard session, answer six honest questions (sleep, food, illness, pain, dizziness, calm), and any 'no' turns it into an easy walk. The Preflight Check: an untested safety habit.

modalities.name: No Two Bouts Alike
modalities.tagline: Every bout a different length, so no rhythm can settle in.
modalities.whatItIs: A coach writes a sequence in which no two hard bouts are the same length, such as 15, 45, 20, 60 and 30 seconds, and you hear each length only as it begins. Where steady training settles into one even rhythm, No Two Bouts Alike denies any rhythm at all; this proposed session runs in a small group or alone, with a new sequence each week.
modalities.coreIdea: Without a repeating pattern to settle into, each bout has to be judged on its own, which is meant to train adaptability rather than steady pacing.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, follow the coach's card for the week: eight hard bouts of different lengths between 15 and 60 seconds, each followed by recovery at least as long as the bout. You do not look ahead on the card; a partner or a timer announces each length just before it starts. Cool down for 10 minutes and note which lengths felt hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get bored by repetitive intervals, and those who want practice in adjusting to whatever comes next.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and pace the longer bouts so you are never all-out for a full minute. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and keep easy days between sessions; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: 15 seconds, then 45, then 20, then 60. A coach writes a sequence where no two bouts match, and you hear each length only as it begins. No Two Bouts Alike: a novel interval idea with no rhythm to settle into.

modalities.name: Quick and Weightless
modalities.tagline: The lightest, fastest movement you can make, with nothing to lift.
modalities.whatItIs: Very fast, very light movement, such as quick feet on the spot, light skipping or fast arm circles, with no weights or load at all: that is Quick and Weightless. Instead of heavy, slow repetitions against resistance, this proposed session chases speed and lightness, moving as quickly as you can while staying springy and relaxed, and it is learned from a coach or a video and then done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Hard effort does not have to feel heavy, and chasing quickness and lightness is meant to give a different, more playful experience of intensity.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, do eight 20-second bouts of the fastest light movement you can manage, alternating quick feet on the spot with fast arm circles or light skipping, with 40 seconds of easy walking between. Keep foot contacts soft and quiet, as if the floor were hot. Finish with a slow walk and gentle stretching.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dislike lifting or feel heavy and sluggish, and anyone who wants a quick, playful session they can do in a small space.
modalities.cautions: Fast footwork can strain calves and ankles, so start with short bouts on a forgiving surface in good shoes, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain and rest between hard days; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Hard intervals that feel light. Quick and Weightless is an experimental idea: 20-second bursts of the fastest, lightest movement you can make (quick feet, skipping, arm circles), nothing to lift, as if the floor were hot.

modalities.name: Count Your Own Seconds
modalities.tagline: Time every bout by counting in your head, then check.
modalities.whatItIs: No watch, app or partner keeps time here: you time each hard bout and each rest by counting in your head, and only check a clock afterward. In Count Your Own Seconds nothing outside you keeps time, keeps you company or tells you what to do; this proposed session can be done anywhere you can move hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping your own time while working hard is a small test of self-reliance, and comparing your count with the clock shows how effort bends your sense of time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Start a stopwatch, put it face down and warm up for 10 minutes by feel. Then do six bouts of what you count as 30 seconds hard, on a bike, up a slope or with fast bodyweight moves, each followed by what you count as 90 seconds easy. At the end, turn the watch over, compare the total with what it should have been, and note the difference.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tied to screens and gadgets during exercise, and anyone curious about how effort changes their sense of time.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and do not let a fast inner count shorten your recoveries: when in doubt, rest longer. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Watch face down, no app, no partner. Time every hard bout and every rest by counting in your head, then check the clock at the end. How much does hard effort bend your sense of time? Count Your Own Seconds would find out. Untested; if unsure, rest more.

modalities.name: Into the Heavy Gear
modalities.tagline: Short, strictly set bouts against heavy resistance, every stroke forced.
modalities.whatItIs: Each hard bout is ridden on a stationary bike set to a heavy, fixed resistance at a slow, prescribed cadence, so every pedal stroke has to be forced round. Into the Heavy Gear is the opposite of qigong's soft, yielding movement: more forceful and even more tightly prescribed than ordinary intervals, with resistance, cadence, bout length and rest all fixed in advance. It borrows the low-cadence, heavy-gear intervals cyclists already use and adds one strict rule, that every number stays fixed for a block of weeks; it is a proposed session, learned from a coach and then done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Where qigong yields and flows, this meets a heavy, unchanging resistance head-on, stroke after stroke, and fixes every number in advance so that nothing is felt out or improvised.
modalities.whatYouDo: Warm up for 10 minutes at light resistance, then set the bike to the heavy level chosen when you learned the session and do eight 20-second bouts at about 60 pedal turns a minute, each stroke pushed hard and smooth, with 100 seconds of very light pedaling between. The resistance, cadence and timing stay exactly as written for a whole block of weeks, and you raise the resistance one step only when all eight bouts are completed cleanly. Cool down for 10 minutes at light resistance.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the feeling of force more than speed, and anyone who wants hard intervals with no impact and nothing left to chance.
modalities.cautions: Heavy pushing raises blood pressure sharply, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, a history of stroke or knee problems, and breathe steadily throughout, never holding your breath. Start at a moderate setting, keep the saddle at the right height and stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp knee pain; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Heavy resistance, 60 turns a minute, every stroke forced round. Into the Heavy Gear sets up an experimental bike session: eight 20-second bouts with every number fixed in advance, and the load goes up only when all eight are clean. Breathe steadily throughout.

modalities.name: Nobody to Follow
modalities.tagline: Six hard moves learned by heart, done alone with nobody to copy.
modalities.whatItIs: In a class or a workout video you copy the person in front; in Nobody to Follow there is no one to copy, so a fixed sequence of six hard moves is learned by heart and done alone, with only an interval timer keeping time. Socializing is built on following and responding to other people, and this proposed session pushes interval training the other way, into a solitary, rigidly set routine that lives in your own memory and body, learned from a coach in two or three sessions.
modalities.coreIdea: Always following someone else's lead can leave you unable to train without them, and carrying one fixed sequence in your own memory is meant to make the session something you can do anywhere, alone, with nothing to watch.
modalities.whatYouDo: A coach teaches you a fixed sequence of six moves, such as squat jumps, mountain climbers, fast step-ups, push-ups, high knees and skaters, checks your form and gives you easier versions of any you need. At home you warm up for 10 minutes, then work through the six in the same order, 30 seconds hard and 60 seconds easy each, twice through, with a timer chiming the changes and no screen, card or music. If you forget the next move, march on the spot until it comes back, and once a month you show the coach the sequence so your form does not drift.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who only exercise when following a class, an app or a video and stall without one, and anyone who wants a hard session they can do anywhere on their own.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and because jumps strain the knees, ankles and pelvic floor, use the coach's low-impact versions until you have built a base. You train alone, so keep a phone within reach for emergencies, and stop at once at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp joint pain; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: No video, no instructor, nobody to copy. Learn six hard moves by heart from a coach, then do them alone at home, 30 seconds each, twice through, with only a timer. Nobody to Follow is an untested idea. Keep a phone near and stop for chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: See It, Then Do It
modalities.tagline: Picture each hard bout in detail, then do exactly that.
modalities.whatItIs: Every hard bout is first played through in the imagination, eyes closed, for about 15 seconds, and then ridden for real on a stationary bike. See It, Then Do It turns attention from scenery and surroundings to a coach-scripted inner picture of each bout. It borrows the mental rehearsal long used in sport and applies it bout by bout inside one proposed interval session.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing a hard effort in the mind's eye just before it starts is meant to make the bout feel familiar and planned, so the body follows a picture instead of a reaction.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a stationary bike, spend the last 15 seconds of each easy recovery pedaling gently with eyes closed, picturing the coming 30-second bout in detail: the start, your posture, the breathing, the last five seconds. Then open your eyes and ride it hard, followed by 90 seconds easy. Repeat six to eight times and cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who freeze up or start chaotically on hard efforts, and anyone who likes to plan before acting.
modalities.cautions: Only close your eyes on a stationary machine, never while running or riding outdoors, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure. Stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and keep easy days between sessions; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: See it, then do it. In this prototype idea, you close your eyes for 15 seconds on a stationary bike and picture the next hard bout in detail (start, posture, breath, finish), then open them and ride it. Six to eight rounds, indoors.

modalities.name: Three Points of Form
modalities.tagline: A partner checks three written form points on every hard bout.
modalities.whatItIs: A coach writes three form points for one machine, for rowing for example 'legs first', 'back stays long' and 'handle to the ribs', and on every hard bout a partner watches and ticks each point that held. Instead of going by how the effort feels from inside, as sensory practice would, Three Points of Form goes by how the movement looks from outside, checked against a fixed standard; this proposed session is learned from the coach once and then done in pairs.
modalities.coreIdea: Form often slips as fatigue builds, frequently without you noticing, so a partner's outside view against the same three written points is meant to show exactly when and how your technique gives way.
modalities.whatYouDo: One partner warms up for 10 minutes on a rowing machine and then rows eight 30-second hard bouts with 90 seconds easy between, while the other watches from the side and ticks each of the three points that held; then you swap, the second partner warming up while the first cools down. The rules are fixed and nobody changes them mid-session: if any point is missed in two bouts in a row, the rest of that partner's bouts are rowed easy. Afterward you look at the cards together to see in which bout each point first slipped.
modalities.whoItsFor: Training partners who want hard intervals with something to learn in them, and people whose technique tends to fall apart when they get tired.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting, high blood pressure or back problems, learn the rowing technique with the coach before going hard, and keep each bout hard but controlled rather than all-out. Stop at once at chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or sharp back pain, whatever the card says; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Legs first, back long, handle to the ribs. Your partner ticks those three points on every hard 30-second row, so you can see the exact bout where tiredness starts to bend your technique. Learn the stroke first; Three Points of Form is untested.

modalities.name: Nothing in Your Ears
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals with no music, only your own breath and steps.
modalities.whatItIs: No music, podcast or headphones: the only soundtrack is your own breathing, footsteps and heartbeat. With no outside beat to follow, Nothing in Your Ears lets both the rhythm and the effort come from your own body; it is a proposed, self-led and fully structured session.
modalities.coreIdea: Without a playlist to carry you, you hear your own rhythm and effort directly, and the pace comes from your body rather than from a beat.
modalities.whatYouDo: Run, row or cycle with no audio at all: warm up for 10 minutes, then do six hard 2-minute bouts with 2 minutes easy between. Listen to the rhythm your steps or strokes fall into on their own, and to the sounds around you, rather than to any beat. In the last bout, notice whether the rhythm changes as you tire.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never exercise without headphones and want to try it unplugged, and anyone who wants to learn to read their own effort.
modalities.cautions: Anyone with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice before hard intervals, and everyone should build up gradually with easy days between sessions. Being unplugged outdoors helps you hear traffic, but still choose safe routes, and stop at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Leave the headphones at home. Six hard 2-minute bouts with no soundtrack but your own breath and footsteps, letting your body set its own rhythm. Nothing in Your Ears: an untested way to hear your effort instead of a beat.
